0.-Preparation.title: 0. Preparation
0.-Preparation.content:
Things to get sorted before we go

Bikes need to be road registered and licenced beyond the Expedition end date.
Original eNatis certificate is essential to travel with owner / driver.
Clearance certificate from police station – x 3 copies. Every Driver of every motorcycle must list every attachment and tool on the bike even extras such as lights.
Don’t leave loose things - Tools, GPS etc. on the bikes - bring them with you or place them in a separate bag for transporting.
Get a clearance certificate from the police that states its not stolen and it belongs to you.
Prepare an authorisation letter confirming a driver can transport it to Namibia for you.

Can the above clearance / letters all be done as one ??


It is up to each bike owner to insure their own bikes and notify their insurer of the trip details.
Mike to confirm bike trailer is insured etc.
Copies of key documents (passports, ID etc.) to be made.
Medical Aid to be notified of the trip.
Bikes and documents delivered to TBA on the TBA for loading; with 4 x labelled Tie-down straps (non Chinese - preferably narrow ratchet), Shock protector.




                  
                  You want to enjoy the whole expedition, right? .... 
                  
                



                  
                  Get your body expedition ready!! ... fitness is very important to ride for 12 days over 1,900kms (that's like the Dakar, only slower). 
                  
                

Big difference riding for 3 days and 12 days of focused active riding!!!
Riding for two weeks in hot sun and Kaokoland terrain is very demanding, and energy margins are thin. So every little bit matters much more than on weekend trips.
Chris Birch after his Dakar, where he didn’t exactly excel. He said the terrain was easy peasy - nothing to compare to roof. But the day in day out grind for two weeks was what made that race really tough.
This type of expedition is similar - of course relatively speaking.
Energy preservation is everything and will be deciding factor between enjoying the trip and/or just pure suffering and bailing out.
Get your butt seasoned and hands hardened!… Go for multiple long outrides
Get some time in soft sand - you’ll thank yourself later.
Get in some technical stuff to build confidence.


                  
                  Injuries and exhaustion will spoil your trip ...  you don't want to end up in the support vehicle and peddling kitchen and campsite duties!!

Visas
Visa requirements for Namibia depend on your nationality, but all travellers need a passport valid for at least six months beyond their stay and with at least three blank pages. Some nationalities can get a visa on arrival, while others must apply online beforehand or through an embassy. All travellers should also have a valid return ticket. 
Key requirements for all visitors

Passport: Must be valid for at least six months after your departure date and have at least three blank pages. 
Return ticket: You must have a valid return or onward ticket. 
Yellow fever vaccination: A yellow fever vaccination certificate is required if arriving from a country with a risk of yellow fever. 

Visa on arrival or advance application

Online application: 
To avoid delays, it is recommended to apply for an e-Visa online before your trip. An online application can be submitted through the MHAISS E-Services Portal
Visa on arrival: 
Some nationalities can get a visa upon arrival at major entry points, but it is still recommended to apply online beforehand. 
Application details: 
You will need a completed application form, a valid passport, and confirmation of accommodation. 

Visa exemptions

Citizens from certain countries, such as Botswana, Kenya, South Africa, and Zimbabwe, do not require a visa for a stay of up to 90 days for tourism, visiting friends/relatives, or business. 
Some countries, including the USA and UK, now require a visa on arrival or an advance e-Visa application as of April 1, 2025.

10.-Day-8---to-Marble-Camp.title: 10. Day 8 - to Marble Camp
10.-Day-8---to-Marble-Camp.content:
A relative short distance (63kms) but an action packed day with striking scenery over the Marienfluss grasslands and rugged mountains that make it a bucket-list experience for serious adventurers.
van Zyl’s pass  is widely regarded as one of Namibia’s toughest 4×4 challenges and often ranked among the more difficult mountain passes in Southern Africa forming a dramatic transition from the high plateaus into the Marienfluss Valley.
Despite its short length, it can take several hours (sometimes a large part of a day) to drive because of technical driving, obstacles and the need to carefully pick lines through rocks.
Travellers advise: take your time and walking tricky sections first to assess lines, placing rocks where needed and using a spotter to guide the driver.
This area is very remote with no cell phone reception, limited access to help and long distances from medical facilities —  more than 600 km to the nearest hospital!

Route


Scenery

































||

Marienfluss

The Marienfluss it is often described as the reward for the effort
After the technical intensity of Van Zyl’s Pass, encountering the fairy-circle-studded grasslands of the Marienfluss often feels like entering a different realm entirely—open, quiet, patterned, and timeless.
The fluss grasslands seems to change with the seasons and the rainfall. When it’s grassy - fairy circles appear.
Fairy circles are fragile ecological features:  Avoid riding / driving through them.
For many Himba and local inhabitants, the circles are not curiosities to be explained away, but features of a living landscape with meaning beyond science.
It is not a destination for speed or sightseeing in the conventional sense, but for immersion.

Overnight stop - Marble Camp

Camping in the Orupembe Conservancy campsite - Marble
Another night of roughing it with home cooked food, and DIY sleeping arrangements.
The sense of isolation is profound; nights are silent except for wind and distant animal sounds.

It has fully equipped campsites (five private screened sites) with braai/barbecue areas and food‐prep counters.
Ablution: There are separate male & female blocks, flush toilets, hot & cold showers.
Hot water is provided via solar heating.
Water: Tap water / basic water supply is present. The site is in a remote area, so don’t assume full infrastructure like grid water pressure everywhere.
Electricity: According to the community-tourism page, this site has no electricity.
Deep-freeze / communal freezer facilities available for use.

So for our expedition: Good infrastructure for camping, but plan as if no mains electricity for vehicle or power-demanding equipment.
Solar lighting, headlamps and power banks will be prudent.

11.-Day-9---to-Puros.title: 11. Day 9 - to Puros
11.-Day-9---to-Puros.content:
A seemingly short distance (primary route - 113kms). Much of this route follows dry riverbeds (ephemeral rivers) such as the Hoarusib so expect a bit slower going.
Travel here means driving in and out of sandy riverbed sections, negotiating soft sand, rock obstacles and braided tracks.
There are alternate routes that are more canyon-like, which would need to be verified for safe and complete passage.
Puros has a community campsite; facilities are basic but a common rendezvous point and often the only reliable fuel point on this section.


Primary Route


About 20 km of open track running on the west side to Khumib river to the D3707 and Orupembe turnoff,
where one jumps into the river and follow it for another 50 km south,
at which point one would jump over a scenic passes - Hoarusib river and follow that another 25 km down to Puros.
Note: The green route below marks double track running on the open plains east of the Khumib river - optional for the vehicles.
Motorcycles will certainly have fun in the river beds

2 - Puros & Hoarusib Riverbed (Vehicle - Vibey)

Puros

Puros conservancy borders the Skeleton Coast Park in Namibia’s Kunene region and the campsite is situated on the banks of the Hoarusib river, for most of the year, this river is a largely dry and dusty, but for the years when there has been generous summer rainfalls, it dramatically changes and makes large parts of this area impassable.
If you are lucky you might catch a glimpse of the elusive grey giants, the Desert elephants, who silently roam this area from the Ugab river. If you are lucky you might even spot them around the campsite as they eagerly seek out Acacia tree seed pods and leaves.
The name Puros originates from the Otjiherero word “omburo” meaning underground water, this area is filled with artesian springs and one of the main attractions for the elephants as they dig deeply into the riverbed in search of fresh water. This area is also frequented by giraffe, Oryx, ostrich, baboon and very occasionally a lion or two.


Overnight stop - Puros Bush Lodge and Camp

Nestled next to the Hoarusib river, the small Himba village of Puros is a true gem of Kaokoland.
The Bush Lodge & Camp is situated a few kilometres upstream under the giant thorn threes that provide well needed shade from the desert sun.
6 chalets & 1 family unit on a self-catering basis.
Additionally pitch your camp in one of our spacious campsites under age old camel thorn trees.
Each site has its own warm water shower and toilet.
Own braai facilites or use the communal facilities at the lapa
Lapa & dining area with bar facilities
Enjoy the vast bird and animal-life that visit us regularly.
What is better than sitting next to your camp-fire with a cold one whilst watching the elephants or giraffes stroll by…
Note the lodge runs on limited solar power. A secure charging station for phones, cameras and other accessories will be available in the manager’s office.

12.-Day-10---to-Ongongo.title: 12. Day 10 - to Ongongo
12.-Day-10---to-Ongongo.content:
A longer day in the saddle (192kms), typically described as a slow, technical 4×4 day rather than a “road drive”.
We start the day riding through the beautiful Puros canyon.
One will spend long sections in dry riverbeds (sand ranging from firm to very soft), with frequent in/out of the river course depending on braiding and obstacles.
Typically why trip times vary wildly.
Permits / gates and controlled access
There is a mention of a permit gate / fee when entering the Hoanib riverbed trail system near Sesfontein (cash payment), where travellers are briefed on rules.
Exact prices change, but the existence of a gate/permit process appears to be a consistent theme.
Wildlife risk
The Hoanib / Puros corridors are specifically known for desert-adapted elephants, and travellers explicitly warn you can “come across elephants at any time” in the river systems.
Recommended to stay as a group.


Primary Route


Scenery highlights

Puros Canyon: Narrow canyon sections with high rock walls and intermittent sandy riverbed driving—often described as one of the most visually dramatic parts of the Puros area.
Lonely man: Sport him - “Consolidate ideas before the meeting”
Transition via Ganamub “Poort”: A “gateway” feel where you drop into/meet the Hoanib corridor.
Hoanib River Valley: Classic desert-river scenery—wide sandy beds, ana trees, and big sky;  sense of remoteness and wildlife potential in the river.


Puros Canyon


Scenery





























|

After the canyon, there is a pretty flat section which can be ridden Dakar style (pinned), all they way down to the Hoanab River. Then head left up the Hoanab river -
For the more chilled sort … as Martin said in his report …



                  
                  On top of the central plain that runs between the two rivers for about 40 - 50 km. Flat featureless vastness in every direction for dozens of km with remote solitary mountains floating on mirage cushions above horizon can have surprisingly uplifting effects on ones soul 
                  
                


Hoanib River

The Hoanib river is one of the 12 ephemeral seasonal rivers in the west of Namibia, and acts as a border between northern Damaraland and Kaokoland.
Measuring 270km’s in length and considering its very low population density it is considered a veritable oasis to the wildlife inhabiting this region.
When dry it teems with large groups of wildlife, all finding respite from the intense day time heat reaching up to 42 degrees celsius.
The riverbed and its giant Ana trees and Leadwood offer large tracts of shade to Oryx, elephant, giraffe and a few lion prides.
The terrain is incredible, the valley being one of the last true wilderness areas in Namibia.
Canyons created in weathered stone by strong winds and water erosion bend and twist their way through the landscape, and it is almost inconceivable that during occasional floods the water levels can be several metres high and last for a few days.
Some years the water makes its way to the mouth in the Atlantic, whilst most of it will seep into the soil and become part of the subsurface aquifer.

Lion habitat

14.-Day-12---Desolation-valley.title: 14. Day 12 - Desolation valley
14.-Day-12---Desolation-valley.content:
And now for something completely barren … The longest stretch of this expedition (233kms).
We will head down the Doros Crater 4wd trail …


The Doros Crater is a large, remote volcanic feature in north-western Namibia, often described as a collapsed volcanic caldera rather than an impact crater, measuring roughly 3–4 km in diameter and rising subtly above the surrounding desert plains; its origin is linked to ancient volcanic activity associated with the Etendeka flood basalts, and today it presents as a broad ring of low hills enclosing a sparsely vegetated interior. Reached only by challenging 4×4 tracks and requiring careful navigation, the Doros Crater is valued less for dramatic relief than for its geological significance, profound isolation, and the sense of deep time it conveys—making it a niche but rewarding destination for experienced Kaokoveld and Damaraland travellers seeking true wilderness rather than conventional landmarks.

Route


Scenery

















||

Divorce pass
“Divorce Pass” in Namibia is a notoriously challenging 4x4 track in the rugged Damaraland region, known for its steep, rocky terrain, rock slides, and sharp climbs/descents, requiring high clearance and careful driving, rewarding adventurers with stunning scenery and a significant sense of achievement. It’s a popular, difficult adventure route for overlanders connecting areas like Twyfelfontein towards the Ugab River, often taking hours to traverse. 
Key Characteristics of Divorce Pass:

Location: Damaraland, Erongo Region, near Brandberg Mountain and Ugab River.
Difficulty: Very rocky, steep, requires high clearance and a 4x4 vehicle; not for the faint-hearted.
Experience: Exciting, adventurous, with opportunities for photography and exploring remote landscapes.
Duration: Can take a significant portion of a day to complete safely. 


Why it’s Called Divorce Pass:

The name reflects the pass’s demanding nature, suggesting it’s a trial that tests relationships and vehicles, similar to the challenges of a divorce itself. 

What to Expect if Driving It:

Vehicle: A proper 4x4 with high clearance is essential.
Preparation: Lower tire pressure for better grip, take your time, and be prepared for slow, careful driving.
Rewards: Breathtakingly beautiful views and an unforgettable adventure.



                  
                  We drove this pass on April 25th after heavy rain, which was already difficult, and had to turn back because of the subsequent blockage by the rather high river... it was quite nerve-wracking, although much easier than the van Zyls Pass. (April 2025) 
                  
                



                  
                  This is a stunning pass but again it must not be under estimated. It is technically difficult and should not be taken lightly. Steep inclines Sharp jagged rocks near cliff passes and can get extremely hot. take your time. and use caution. it will take you the better part of 3 hours to complete so be aware you have sufficient time to get in and out. The views are stunning and once completed it is a significant achievement. (March 2024) 
                  
                



                  
                  Definitely set aside a full day for this route. We drove from north to south, and the last 6 km alone took over 1.5 hours. It's essential to have someone go ahead on difficult sections. We had to fill in some deep potholes with stones to drive over them. Otherwise, it's a fantastic route with breathtaking scenery. We saw fresh elephant tracks everywhere in Goantagab. A little tip: You don't necessarily have to drive over Divorca Pass to get to Brandberg Mine. You can also stay in Goantagab from Doros Crater to reach the mine. (January 2021) 
                  
                


Divorce Pass is a mountain pass at an elevation of 401m (1,315ft) above the sea level, located in the Kunene region of Namibia, in southern Africa.

19.-Buitepos-border-post.title: 19. Buitepos border post
19.-Buitepos-border-post.content:
Here are the key points and recent updates on crossing at Buitepos Border Post (between Namibia and Botswana) and bringing a South African-registered motorcycle into Namibia via that or similar crossings (note: Buitepos is more commonly the Namibia-Botswana border, so if you meant the Namibia-South Africa border please check the specific post).

✅ Things we must do


We all need valid passports, motorcycle’s registration papers, and if not the registered owner, a letter of authority. These are general border requirements.


Use the correctly registered plate (South African registration), carry the ZA sticker.


On entry into Namibia we must obtain a Temporary Import Permit (TIP) for a foreign-registered vehicle (even if it’s from a SACU country). The form is provided by the Namibia Revenue Agency (or similar authority). (Form)


For foreign-registered vehicles (i.e. outside Namibia) including motorcycles we will need to pay any required road user / cross-border charges at the border post or at the associated authority – e.g., the Road Fund Administration (RFA) in Namibia notes this for foreign-registered vehicles. (Road Fund Administration)



⚠️ Specifics for Buitepos / Notes & caveats


According to the “Namibia Handbook” (though somewhat older) the Buitepos/Mamuno post (Namibia-Botswana) lists opening hours 07:00-24:00. If you meant Buitepos as the Botswana/Namibia border, check that you are allowed to bring South Africa-registered vehicles via that route and re-export them properly.


The RFA cross-border charges document notes that all foreign-registered vehicles entering Namibia must pay CBC (Cross Border Charge) and obtain the permit at the border. Buitepos is listed under “Trans-Kalahari (Buitepos)”.


For SACU country vehicles (i.e., South Africa vehicles) some sources say a Carnet is not required. E.g., a blog says: “Entering Namibia from SA or vice-versa does not require a TIP or carnet for a SADC registered vehicle.” However this needs confirmation and may differ depending on motorcycle vs car, or length of stay.


The official Temporary Import Permit form and directive say “A temporary import permit must be produced on demand, is valid for the duration of the visit, and must be handed over upon departure.”



🧭 What this means for our motorcycle adventure trip


At Buitepos plan to stop at customs/immigration, and at the RFA (or relevant Namibia road authority) to pay any CBC/road-user charge and get the permit.


When entering Namibia, carry all vehicle documents, pay the required fees, obtain the permit, and keep it with the motorcycle.


On exiting Namibia, ensure we hand back the temporary import permits (or have it stamped) to show we have re-exported the vehicle correctly.


Even though some sources say SACU-registered vehicles may not need a carnet, we should double-check with the local border post and confirm for motorcycles, especially if we intend to ride via remote areas (like conservancies) and return to South Africa.


Because Buitepos is a border between Namibia and Botswana, our route starts in South Africa, we will cross into Botswana first then Namibia — we need to ensure each border crossing is compliant.


Check the fee scale: e.g., older handbook shows for motorcycles/quadricycles the entry charge: “R 188 for motorcycles …” when entering Namibia.



🔍 Recommendation
Before we depart, contact the Buitepos Border Post (Namibia side) or the nearest Namibian customs office to confirm:

That the permit/temporary import process for a South African-registered motorcycle is the same as for cars.
The exact fee amount for a motorcycle for your length of stay.
Any special conditions for remote travel (into conservancies, etc).
The opening hours and whether they can handle registration/permits for motorcycles.


Fee schedule
Here are the latest published fee schedules and relevant details for vehicle cross-border charges (CBC) and related permits for foreign-registered vehicles entering Road Fund Administration (RFA) jurisdiction in Namibia (including via the Buitepos Border Post).

✅ Key published fees


The RFA’s official “Charges – Cross-Border Charges (Entry Fees) for Foreign-Registered Vehicles (Effective 1 May 2024)” list shows:

For motorcycles, motor tricycles, motor quadracycles, caravans & light trailers drawn by Type 2 vehicles: NAD 283.
For motor cars, single and double cab goods vehicles (bakkies), 2x4 and 4x4 goods vehicles: NAD 445.
For heavier categories there are higher fees (light goods vehicles, heavy trucks etc).



The RFA site confirms that the CBC (Cross Border Charge) must be paid by foreign-registered vehicles at the border post RFA office.


A travel information site states for vehicles entering Namibia: “The CBC costs N$445 (as of March 2025) and is valid for three months.”



⚠️ Interpretation & practical implications for you (motorcycle from South Africa)


Since your case is a motorcycle registered in South Africa entering Namibia and then returning: the published fee of NAD 283 (as of 1 May 2024) applies to motorcycles/ tricycles etc.


The fee is valid at least until updated and must be paid at the relevant border post RFA office (e.g., Buitepos for the Trans-Kalahari route) when you enter.


You’ll need to carry the permit/certificate issued after payment in the vehicle at all times. Non-compliance may incur fines (e.g., up to NAD 4,000 for missing permit) according to RFA.


Check validity: some sources say the permit (CBC) may be valid for up to three months.


Because your vehicle is South African-registered (a SACU country), although some blogs suggest fewer burdens, the official fee schedule above still appears to apply for “foreign-registered vehicles” (i.e., non-Namibian). So plan on paying.


At Buitepos (Trans-Kalahari route) there is an RFA CBC office as listed on RFA’s site.



✅ What you should do


On entering Namibia via Buitepos, stop at the RFA CBC office, declare your motorcycle, pay the NAD 283 fee (confirm current rate there), get the permit/certificate.


Keep the permit with you on the bike throughout your stay.


On exiting Namibia, present the permit to RFA/Border post to show proper re-exportation of the vehicle and compliance.


Check with the border post just before your trip to confirm if there have been any updates or changes to the fee (since fees can change).


Ensure your other vehicle/driver documents are in order (registration papers, ZA sticker, insurance, letter of authority if needed, etc).

Up the Umaruru river

We will confirm the conditions of the riverbeds prior to doing this and other sections of the route, but assuming conditions are good, we’ll travel about 80kms inside the Umaruru riverbed, hang right and head down to Spitzkoppe.
There is a good chance the support vehicles can follow on the same route. If not, there is an alternate route available, but super corrugated, I’m told.
We should leave at first light to give us as much time as possible to enjoy the route and to get to Spitzkoppe early as possible - to enjoy this magical place.

Spitzkoppe

The Spitzkoppe is a group of bald granite peaks or inselbergs. The sheer size with voluptuous curves makes this cluster formation so intriguing. The granite is more than 120 million years old and the highest outcrop rises about 1,728 metres above sea level. The peaks stand out dramatically from the flat surrounding plains.



They have great expansive campsites! There are nice outdoor showers at reception and ablutions spread around. We will have all we need so we were good to camp and have fun riding / driving around.

Organ Pipes

Formed as molten lava intruded into older rock (slate/shale), then cooled and contracted, fracturing in such a regular, polygonal pattern. Estimated to be around 130–150 million years old, making it a relic of ancient volcanic activity in the region. Over time, erosion exposed these basalt/dolerite columns, creating the dramatic “organ-pipe” effect - The result is striking: a natural “cathedral” of stone, often described as one of the more spectacular examples of basalt columnar jointing in southern Africa — a kind of geological monument to Earth’s volcanic past.

9.-Day-7---to-van-Zyl's-camp.title: 9. Day 7 - to van Zyl's camp
9.-Day-7---to-van-Zyl's-camp.content:
This where the exploration really gets interesting - where the feeling of the wilderness takes root, from a landscape, remoteness and riding perspective.
Only 145kms but will take several hours going through this very unique countryside.
The first 80kms is easy going and also the last easy going section for many kms.
The next 65kms is beautiful riding across jeep tracks heading toward the infamous van Zyl’s pass.
The D3703 is known as the “Tyre Eater Pass”.
Many roads (tracks) in Kaokaland have broken up rocks with very sharp edges, deposited by the South African Defence Force so that their vehicles could supply the Guard Posts along the Cunene.
From Van Zyl’s up through the Marienfluss, is another danger area where the long grass gets caught up in the exhaust pipes and catches alight especially in petrol driven vehicles which run much hotter than diesel.

Namibia 2026 Expedition






























































CONTENTS0. Preparation1. Getting there2. Daily schedule3. Day 1 - to Spitzkoppe4. Day 2 - to Brandberg5. Day 3 - to Palmwag6. Day 4 - to Khowarib20. Lone men of NamibiaVetenary constraints and considerations29. River crossing mitigation30. Latest Country Information31. The River systems

Summary of the Expedition

This Expedition will take us through some of the most geographically diverse and sparsely occupied terrain in Namibia … Damaraland and Kaokoland (the Erongo and Kunene regions); we’ll be riding through and seeing some unusual landmarks like Spitzkoppe, Brandberg, Epupa Falls, Van Zyl’s pass, the Marienfluss, Purros Canyon, Kowharib Schlucht, Desolation valley and a bunch more. The best part for bikers … you will be witnessing changing conditions right under you feet every day.
While the terrain is often rough, we’ve opted for a mix of roughing it in the open and the occasional luxury lodging.  Unlike some solo travellers without support, we’ve opted to go for a little more comfort and piece of mind, making travelling lighter and agile to enjoy the time in the saddle and hopefully less fatigue in the sandy, fesh-fesh and rocky conditions. We will be supported by three vehicles who will bring along all the goodies to complete the safety, camping, catering and backup facilities we’ll need.


Map and routes














USEFUL LINKS<~~o0o0o0o EXPEDITION ROUTES o0o0o0o~~>Tracks4Africa Map - A good place to look around


                  
                  We will have to keep weather conditions prior to our trip in mind, it could influence the routes. Vetenary and border regulations also need to be checked.
                  
                












EXPEDITION SECTION.

12 days of magical terrain - travelling around 1,900kms to and from Henties bay. It is a true dual sport adventure in one of the most beautiful and fascinating places on earth. One needs a  degree of sand and technical riding skill and experience covering some sand and rocky mountain passes during the trip. Fitness will play an important role as fatigue is likely to creep in at some point.
Bikes will be trailered into and out of Namibia. At the appropriate time, you will be notified where and when to deliver your bikes, your kit and all the mandatory documentation - of which there is a crap load.
This expedition is prepared on a cost covering basis. We have limited this to 10 riders, all riders contributing equally to the costs of the fuel,  accommodation, supplies, spares etc. Support crew will contribute to their accommodation, supplies and related costs.
We will arrange, where possible, spares etc. on a return basis.





























































Included in this expedition:- All the accommodation in Namibia (mostly camping) / Bring your own Stretcher, sleeping bag & camping chair  - All cutlery, crockery, cooking utilities & equipment- Breakfast, lunch packs & dinner (eating out where available) - Fresh water and refreshments  - Fridge / Freezer - Ice when available  - Backup and recovery vehicles  - Medical support / First-aid kit and assistance from George & Andrew- Aerial evacuation arrangements with an Evacuation Company. ???  - Backup  fuel for bikes in areas where no fuel is available. We’ll all fill wherever possible. (budget around R2000/pp) - Tracks / Routes to upload to your GPS.  - General Tools. (). - Tyre Air Compressor.  - Puncture repair equipment.- Limited bike spares and accessories.- 2 X Satellite phones (For emergencies in the remote areas, where there is no Cell / Wi-Fi)- Walkie talkies for Support vehicles & Sweeper.- Riders recommended to use intercom system.


                  
                  Each biker / biker buddy should carry one set of basic tools and tyre repair stuff 
                  
                


Regional map

Some arb information about the region …
Erongo Region
Erongo Region
This region comprises the Swakopmund magisterial district up to the Ugab river and includes the enclave of Walvis Bay, former Damaraland south of the Ugab river, and the Omaruru and Karibib magisterial districts. The region comprises of six constituencies: Omaruru, Karibib, Brandberg, Arandis, Swakopmund, Walvis Bay.
This region is named after the Erongo mountain, a well known landmark in Namibia and in this area. All the main centres within this region, excepting south of former Damaraland, are connected by tarred roads. Gravel roads link this this part with either Omaruru or Swakopmund.
The inclusion of former South Damaraland is necessitated by various services for this part which originate in Omaruru. Postal and telecommunications services for Omatjette, Okombahe and Uis are maintained from Omaruru. Veterinary services for these areas are provided by the State Veterinarian based at Omaruru.
The Omaruru, Karibib and Okombahe/Uis/Tsubeses areas are all situated in a semi-arid farming region and have a homogenous farming pattern, which is mostly stock-raising. It also combines communal farming with commercial farming.
Various mining operations occur within this region at places such as  Navachab
and on a smaller scale at places surrounding Uis and the desert area.


                  
                  Info
                  
                

Facilities such as hospitals and clinics, the supply of electricity and telecommunication services are, with a few exceptions, well established.
Medical services are rendered at the clinics of Omatjette, Okombahe, and Uis by medical personnel and private doctors stationed at Omaruru. The main hospital centre for this area is in Omaruru.



Kunene Region
Kunene Region
This region comprises the western part of former Ovambo, Koakoland, Damaraland north of the Ugab river and the Magisterial District of Outjo. The region has been divided into the following six constituencies: Ruacana, Opuwo, Sesfontein, Khorixas, Kamanjab and Outjo.
This region is named after the Kunene river which forms the north-western border of this particular region. With its large supply of water and its hydro-electric plant, this river will play an increasingly important role in Namibia. 
At its main centres, the region has facilities such as clinics and hospitals and electrical power supply.
